name: sollya
desc: Library for safe floating-point code development
why: A rigorous floating-point toolkit with its own language for polynomial approximation and certified error bounds.

brief.what_it_is: Sollya is a tool environment and a library for developing safe floating-point code. It has its own scripting language, adapted to analysing numerical programs in the way a computer algebra system is. It computes certified infinity-norm error bounds, runs a fast Remez algorithm for minimax polynomials, and evaluates composed functional expressions with multi-precision, faithful rounding on top of MPFR. It can also generate CRlibm-style C code for approximation polynomials along with a Gappa proof. The homepage describes it as particularly aimed at automated implementation of mathematical floating-point libraries (libm). The brew entry lists a single executable, sollya.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says it is targeted at the automatized implementation of mathematical floating-point libraries (libm), where approximation error has to be bounded safely rather than estimated.
brief.how_it_works: The homepage names the main pieces but does not explain the internals: a certified infinity (supremum) norm for safe error bounds, a fast Remez algorithm for minimax polynomials, a multi-precision evaluator for composed expressions that extends MPFR, and a polynomial implementer that emits CRlibm-style C code with a matching Gappa proof. It also offers interfaces for extending Sollya with your own code.
brief.install_notes: Building from source needs a C compiler (e.g. gcc), a C++ compiler (e.g. g++), GMP, MPFR, MPFI, FPLLL and libxml2. Bison and Flex are also needed to build from the git repository. Gnuplot is strongly recommended for the plot and externalplot commands but is optional. The site says Sollya is packaged directly for Debian and Ubuntu. A weekly git snapshot is offered as an alternative to stable releases, and a third-party Python interface exists (see the GitLab link on the homepage, which I did not open).
brief.standout: It is a numerical-analysis language and toolkit rather than a library you call from C: you write scripts that search for polynomial approximations and prove their error bounds, and it can emit C code and Gappa proofs for libm-style functions. The homepage also offers an explicit citation (Chevillard, Joldeş and Lauter, ICMS 2010).
brief.status: quiet. The last stable release listed is 8.0, dated March 29, 2022. The page footer says 'Last update: 2025-03-21'. A weekly snapshot is listed as 'dated from 2026-10-19', which does not match the page's own update date, so I could not confirm recent activity. The homepage gives no commit history.
brief.caveats: The homepage fetch gave no command syntax, so commands_seen is empty; the documentation (PDF and online) was linked but I did not fetch it. The license is CeCILL-C, a French free-software license, and the site itself warns that the software may be complicated to use and is aimed at developers and experienced professionals. Building from source has a long dependency list (GMP, MPFR, MPFI, FPLLL, libxml2). The site's own description is also not fully current, since it cites copyright dates of 2006-2022 for the tool.
